problems.description: Duplicates the project's existing telemetry/messaging infrastructure: live.py already publishes to Redis pub/sub and admin/server.py serves telemetry over SSE. A second, standalone WebSocket broadcast stack (aiohttp + websockets) is redundant and unintegrated with that path.
New root-level server.py diverges from the module map layout; telemetry lives under admin/server.py (Flask), so this parallel implementation at the repo root bypasses established structure.
threading.Lock on the client registry is unnecessary in a single-threaded asyncio server; a plain dict (or a small asyncio-guarded structure) would be simpler.
_broadcast awaits ws.send sequentially, so a slow or backpressured client stalls delivery to all other clients.
No limits on incoming message size, rate, or total registered clients, so unbounded memory/DOS risk on the broadcast loop.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: ClientRegistry, broadcast, handler, and main are decoupled and readable
Full type hints on all public signatures and snake_case functions, matching stated conventions
Graceful shutdown via ws_server.close + runner.cleanup; ConnectionClosed handled during sends
Solid test coverage including sender-exclusion and direct-message edge cases
commit_reviews.summary: Well-written, well-tested standalone WebSocket server, but it replicates existing Redis pub/sub + SSE telemetry and sits outside the project's module layout, adding redundant architecture despite clean code. Note: convention measurement (0.89, 3 violations) aligns with my view of the style; the listed app.py/test_server.py PascalCase violations and the +3 files imply a third diff file not shown here, which I could not independently verify.

problems.description: In _broadcast, get_all() materializes the full client dict even when a channel filter is used, and get_subscribers() iterates all subscription sets; a channel->subscriber map lookup would be O(subscribers) instead of O(clients). Minor at current scale.
Channel-broadcast messages do not include the channel name in the outgoing payload, so recipients cannot distinguish which channel a message arrived on when subscribed to multiple channels.
Cognitive complexity +17 (per SonarQube); _broadcast now branches on channel/exclude/client-missing and could be split into a channel-route vs broadcast-route path for readability.
Convention score 0.89 with 3 violations (module-level constants in server.py should be UPPER_CASE; PascalCase class naming flagged in app.py and test_server.py). Score matches the reported 0.89.

strengths: Subscriptions live in ClientRegistry alongside _clients, respecting the existing lock discipline and lifecycle (cleanup on remove()).
subscribe/unsubscribe message types extend the existing handler dispatch without special-casing the protocol.
Good test coverage: subscribe-and-receive, unsubscribe stops delivery, channel message only to subscribers, plus registry fixture cleanup for _subscriptions.
REST endpoints (/channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers) mirror the existing /health pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested channel-subscription extension that follows the existing ClientRegistry/handler/HTTP patterns, with only minor efficiency and naming nits.

problems.description: _deliver_from_redis re-implements the target/channel/broadcast fanout already present in _broadcast, creating two delivery code paths that must be kept in sync; this duplication is the main driver of the +22 cognitive complexity and +1 smell.

Redis/relay operations are fired as fire-and-forget asyncio.create_task calls (register_client, _publish_and_persist) with no try/except or await; if Redis is down or store.save_message fails, messages are dropped silently and exceptions surface as unhandled task errors with no retry.
Three convention violations per measurement: non-PascalCase classes in app.py and test_server.py, and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in server.py (convention score 0.89).

_deliver_from_redis persists every remote message via store.save_message even though the originating server already persisted it, so each server instance writes its own copy; confirm MessageStore is shared or per-instance to rule out duplicate/divergent message history.

The Redis relay has no authentication or channel authorization; any client that can reach the pub/sub can subscribe to channels or inject messages, though this may be acceptable for a local/experiment deployment.

strengths: Redis lifecycle (connect, subscribe, publish, close) is cleanly encapsulated in a RedisBroker class with idempotent reconnect and full async resource cleanup (unsubscribe/reset/close).
Cross-server dedup via _origin_server identity prevents echo loops when servers relay each other's messages.
Persistence is routed through a single _publish_and_persist entry point, keeping the write path consistent for broadcast, direct, and channel messages.
Follows existing module-level singleton and handler-message-loop patterns already established by registry/broadcast, so it integrates rather than replacing the surrounding architecture.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid integration commit that cleanly adds cross-server Redis relay plus persistence on top of the existing websocket server, with modest maintainability debt from duplicated fanout logic and unhandled fire-and-forget tasks reflected in the +22 cognitive complexity and +1 smell.

compounding_issues: Seed codebase is a Flask Todo API (app.py) but the story is a WebSocket notification service; session 1 abandoned the seed and the orphaned app.py was never deleted or integrated, persisting as dead code through all commits
Runtime state committed to git: messages.db binary and __pycache__/*.pyc files appear in every commit; the final two 'Session 3 (continued)' commits contain ONLY messages.db churn (e7a4f46, 5170302)
Session 3 timed out after 900s (recorded as 'Session 3 failed: Timeout after 900s'), aborting the story at 3 of 5 planned sessions — sessions 4 (refactor) and 5 (rate limiting/history) never ran

Session 3 explicitly required integration tests for Redis pub/sub and persistence, but test_server.py is byte-identical to session 2 (md5 match, 0 diff lines) — new broker.py/store.py have zero test coverage

The Redis client-subscription keys written by set_client_subscriptions() are never read back for routing; cross-server delivery still uses the local registry, leaving the 'client connection state in Redis' requirement half-implemented
Fire-and-forget asyncio.create_task() calls for broker.register_client() and _publish_and_persist() with no exception handling — silent failure risk on Redis/SQLite errors
key_decisions: WebSocket-first architecture (websockets lib) with a thread-safe ClientRegistry and a stable JSON envelope {type, payload, timestamp} supporting broadcast/direct/system
Registry-level channel subscription model added in session 2 (subscribe/unsubscribe message types + /channels REST endpoints), preserving session-1 behavior
Redis pub/sub message backbone on a single 'messages' channel with an _origin_server UUID check to prevent echo delivery across server instances
SQLite (aiosqlite) persistence layer with a single messages table and env-driven config (REDIS_URL, DATABASE_URL) for broker/store connections
Local-first delivery pattern: broadcast locally then publish-and-persist to Redis, with _deliver_from_redis() delivering remote-originated messages only
story_review.trajectory_description: The arc is strong at the start and collapses in the final session. Session 1 was a clean, test-first greenfield: a well-structured WebSocket server with 9 passing tests and a sensible ClientRegistry/health-endpoint design. Session 2 was a disciplined feature addition — channels and subscriptions were added with correct locking, 8 new tests (17 total), and no regressions. Session 3 then stalled badly: the Redis+SQLite integration landed as one oversized 261-line insertion, was split across three commits (the last two being pure messages.db artifact churn), omitted the required integration tests entirely, and ultimately hit the 900s timeout, terminating the story mid-integration with two planned sessions never attempted. Code quality peaked at session 2 and degraded into an unfinished, untested, artifact-polluted session 3.
story_review.summary: A promising greenfield and clean feature-addition start was undermined by an incomplete, testless, and timeout-aborted Redis/SQLite integration session that left the 5-session story only 60% executed with runtime artifacts committed to git.
